newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-Kellogg's earnings beat forecasts, stock jumps.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Kellogg's earnings beat forecasts, stock jumps.

text.p: Kellogg Co. said Friday that earnings more than doubled in the second quarter, easily surpassing expectations on Wall Street, as the company rebounded from the effects of last year's bruising price wars.

The nation's largest breakfast cereal maker said gains in its share of the competitive, $9 billion market helped push earnings to $163.6 million, or 79 cents a share, in the quarter. The results easily outpaced profits of $78.1 million, or 37 cents a share, a year earlier.
The company also announced a 2-for-1 stock split and raised its quarterly dividend.
The news boosted Kellogg stock, which jumped $5.125 to $97 in late trading on the New York Stock Exchange, after hitting a 52-week high of $97.75 early in the session.
Excluding one-time charges, Kellogg earned 83 cents a share, beating average forecasts of 73 cents a share, according to First Call, which tracks estimates.
The results stood in sharp contrast to the company's performance a year earlier, when price cuts by major cereal makers took a toll on Kellogg's bottom line.

"Wonderful. Well above expectations," said Goldman Sachs analyst Nomi Ghez, who had forecast earnings of 75 cents a share. "I have to believe that this shows that Kellogg is back on its feet," Ghez added.

Kellogg said sales rose 4 percent to $1.72 billion from $1.65 billion. Global sales volume climbed 14 percent following the acquisitition last December of Lender's Bagels. Excluding Lender's, volume rose 8 percent.

Kellogg said its share of the domestic market hit 33.8 percent in the quarter, continuing recent steady improvement. The company's share was 33.2 percent in the first quarter, 32.9 percent in the fourth quarter and 32.6 percent in the second and third quarters of last year.
Kellogg's convenience foods business, which includes Nutri-Grain bars, increased by a double-digit rate in the second quarter.
The company, based in Battle Creek, Mich., said its U.S. sales volume rose more than six percent in the second quarter.

Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette analyst William Leach said Kellogg's gains in the second quarter were helped by easy comparisons with last year, when U.S. cereal sales fell 4 percent and international sales were little changed.
Kellogg said domestic cereal growth was aided by its two newest cereals -- Honey Crunch Corn Flakes and Cocoa Frosted Flakes -- which account for 2 percent to 3 percent of the cereal market.
Kellogg also said it was extending its Rice Krispies line by introducing Razzle Dazzle Rice Krispies cereal, which is expected to hit grocery stores nationwide Sept. 1.

Looking ahead, analysts said they expect Kellogg will increase marketing spending in the second half of 1997. In the second half of 1996, Kellogg had reduced spending as a result of cereal price cuts.
"We still think we are in an exciting business category," Joseph Stewart, senior vice president of corporate affairs, said of the U.S. cereal industry.
He added that while the U.S. cereal industry overall is growing by about 1.4 percent, Kellogg expects it could grow at a rate of 2 percent "over time."
This would be below its historic growth rate of 3 percent, but an improvement from a relatively flat performance in 1996.
In addition to the 2-for-1 stock split, Kellogg raised its quarterly dividend to 22.5 cents a share from 21 cents.
